clean_text: Exposing the Hijack: Abhijeet Dipke, CJP, and the Alleged Misuse of Sonam Wangchuk at the Jantar Mantar NEET Protest On 18 July 2026, at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site, a woman allegedly threw blue ink at Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). The incident occurred hours after Delhi Police shifted climate activist Sonam Wangchuk to Safdarjung Hospital following his 20-day hunger strike. Dipke, who had just announced his own indefinite fast, responded on X: "Blue is my colour… Jai Bhim!" The detained woman later told Aaj Tak and The Tribune that she threw the ink after witnessing what she described as mockery of Lord Shri Ram and Sita Maiya on stage. Calling herself a "staunch Sanatani," she alleged the protest had shifted from demanding NEET reforms to promoting identity politics through repeated "Jai Bhim" slogans. She also claimed CJP was "using Sonam Wangchuk" for political messaging, similar to how Anna Hazare was allegedly used in earlier movements. The woman further alleged that Dipke's supporters assaulted her before police intervened. These remain her personal claims and have not been independently verified. News reports confirm only that a scuffle occurred after the ink throw and that police detained her. Separately, Hindu Janajagruti Samiti (HJS) and Supreme Court lawyers also complained about stage content. They objected to remarks by comedian Kunal Kamra concerning Lord Shri Ram and to a performance featuring Faiz Ahmed Faiz's lyrics, alleging both hurt Hindu sentiments. FIRs were demanded against those involved. Dipke's "Blue is my colour… Jai Bhim!" response reinforced the Ambedkarite symbolism already visible at the protest. While the agitation began over alleged NEET irregularities, critics argue it increasingly blended student issues with ideological messaging. Sonam Wangchuk's respected image gave the movement credibility, but questions have since been raised over whether his presence was politically leveraged. clean_text: Nine years ago, S Anitha became the first victim of NEET in Tamil Nadu, and one of the most prominent faces of Tamil Nadu’s fight against NEET. In 2017, the 17-year-old from Ariyalur had scored 1,176 out of 1,200 marks in her Class 12 Tamil Nadu State Board exams. Her medical cut-off score was 196.75 out of 200 — marks that would have placed her among medical aspirants under Tamil Nadu’s earlier admission system. But that year, NEET became mandatory for medical admissions. Anitha, who had prepared through the state-board syllabus, could not secure a medical seat through the national entrance exam. She became one of the earliest voices opposing NEET in Tamil Nadu, arguing that a common entrance test would disadvantage students from rural areas, government schools and marginalised communities. Anitha’s brother S. Manirathnam, who has now joined the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, says her fight was deeply personal. He says Anitha was raised by their father, a daily wage labourer, after their mother died when she was seven. He recalls that Anitha wanted to become a doctor because their mother’s death due to an illness had shaped her dream of entering medicine. “She wanted to become a doctor because she had seen the suffering caused by the lack of medical care,” Manirathnam said, recalling his sister’s journey. Anitha joined the legal battle against NEET and became one of the petitioners before the Supreme Court, seeking relief for Tamil Nadu students. The Court did not grant the exemption sought by the state, and days later, on 1 September 2017, Anitha died by suicide at her home in Ariyalur. Speaking about the impact of NEET on his family, Manirathnam said, “NEET has destroyed my family.” Years later, he has joined the CJP protest, saying Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET began with students like Anitha, who questioned whether a single national entrance exam could account for the inequalities faced by students across the country. @hey_eshwar reports.

The CJP 'cockroach' protests, the NEET leak, and the 20 July protests: what's happened so far, and why it won't blow over (compiled off-ground; reporting, footage, and argument. Doing my bit.) Before the anchors get to it: asking your government why a national medical exam ended up for sale is not terrorism, not sedition, and not a war on Hinduism. It is citizens complaining and pursuing accountability. The Indian state has spent 2026 insisting otherwise, and that is the first tell. When a government answers "where did my exam go" with "who funds you" and "why do you hate the nation," it has quietly confessed that it would rather put your loyalty on trial than its own competence. So keep the loyalty test where it belongs, in the bin. This is not about anyone’s god, whether Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, or none of the above. A government is not a temple, and a leader who keeps hiding behind one has already shown you their priorities. # The record, briefly In May, the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, called unemployed young Indians "cockroaches" and their critics "parasites"; a graduate named Abhijeet Dipke replied, "what if all the cockroaches came together?", and within days the Cockroach Janta Party had 21 million followers and a mascot the judiciary had thoughtfully supplied free of charge. The same month, the NEET medical entrance papers were allegedly leaked and sold, forcing hundreds of thousands to re-sit. By 6 June, the students wanted the Education Minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, gone and the leak investigated, and they added compensation for the families of students who died by suicide and repair of an examination system that had failed them. On 20 July, the first day of the monsoon session, they marched from Jantar Mantar towards Parliament as Chalo Sansad. Sonam Wangchuk, the Ladakh activist, fasted for 26 days and ended it on 24 July (The Guardian). The police used tear gas, batons and, in some instances, threw stones; Human Rights Watch counted more than a hundred injured students, one young woman critical, officers in plain clothes, and riot police who had removed their name tags (HRW, 23 July 2026). # The machinery works. The question is where it points. Here is what should worry the people in charge, and it is not a chant. The Indian state is not weak; it is selective. It can move at extraordinary speed when a comedian tells a bad joke, as it did over India’s Got Latent circus of 2025, and at no speed at all when a national examination is stolen. A dirty punchline earns FIRs across three states and a Supreme Court hearing; a leaked NEET paper that priced the futures of hundreds of thousands earns a re-sit, and anyone who complains in the street gets trashed and branded a terrorist or an "anti-national" by the TV watchdogs, to drown out what the young are actually demanding. Meanwhile the prime-time anchors have located the true threat to the republic: 22-year-olds holding signboards. A foreign hand has reportedly been found; a foreign hand is always found; it is as dependable as the ratings. A government reveals its real priorities not in its manifesto but in its reflexes, and those reflexes are now on the record for an international audience. India sits 157th of 180 on RSF’s 2026 World Press Freedom Index, inside the "very serious" band (RSF, 30 April 2026); in my opinion, that ranking is earned, not accidental. # Why this one does not simply blow over Delhi tends to assume these things burn themselves out, and usually it is right. Three reasons this one is harder to wait out. First, the precedent runs the wrong way for the government. This is the same state that spent a year branding the 2020-21 farmers’ protests as foreign-funded theatre and then quietly repealed all three farm laws. It is the state that sat through the anti-CAA demonstrations, and, a generation earlier, the JP movement that helped end the Emergency. Second, you cannot lathi-charge the youth, the largest chunk of your population. This is the largest youth mobilisation since the farmers, in a country whose median age is 28, organised by 21 million people who needed no party, no leader and no permit to find each other. Repression does not scale against numbers like that. You can clear a crowd from a road. You cannot clear a generation from the electoral roll. Third, and most dangerous of all, these are the government’s own people. The aspirational young who were promised a global power and a golden decade, the ones whose enthusiasm gave the majority its shine, are the same ones whose exams were sold and whose cars are being quietly corroded by an E20 fuel rollout that arrived years early and cheaper by exactly zero rupees (Al Jazeera, 15 July 2026). A government does not fear its opponents working it out. It fears its base doing the arithmetic. # What actually has to happen now Three things decide whether this becomes a change of government or a wistful thread in two years. Hold the line, and hold discipline. The quickest way to hand the government its exit is a burning bus at nine o’clock on prime time, and the provocateurs know it. The man filmed threatening protesters that he would tell the police they had torn his daughter’s clothes was not there by accident. Every student who sits down under a baton and films instead of swinging does more damage to the state’s story than any thrown stone could. Rage is a trap and so is boredom. The movement wins by being impossible to caricature, and by staying peaceful. Document everything, and refuse to let it be filed away. The name tags came off for a reason. The plain clothes were worn for a reason. The internet was cut for a reason. The answer to a state that manages the evidence is a public that keeps its own copy: the flag thrown to the ground, the student beaten while shielding another, the head wound, the tear gas fired at point-blank range, all archived, dated and undeletable. Memory is the one thing the machinery cannot summon before a commission. Name the systems, not just the ministers. A resignation is a scalp, not a repair. The demands that survive contact with reality are structural: an examination body that cannot be bought, riot police who keep their names on their chests, a government that cannot flip a state’s internet off on a whim, and an independent reckoning for what happened on 20 July. Ask for the plumbing, not the trophy. # The tell It needs a government to do the dull and honest work of governing and to survive the indignity of being asked to show its work. That is what makes the crackdown so revealing. A confident state answers the question. An anxious one takes the name tags off its officers, cuts the internet, and gambles that 21 million people will lose interest before the next election. They will not. We, the cockroaches, were named by a judge who meant it as an insult, and we kept the name, because we already understand the one lesson every strongman learns too late: the insect under the boot tends to outlast the boot. He has to win every single year until 2029. We only have to be still standing when the lights come back on. What this movement is asking for is not radical, and it is not new. It is the pile of reforms every government has promised and quietly shelved: an examination system that cannot be bought, so that a leaked paper and a rich buyer do not undo a student’s decade of work. Riot police who keep their names on their chests, so that a baton to a boy’s head has an owner. A state that cannot switch off a city’s internet on a whim to police its own embarrassment. An education minister who resigns when the system he runs collapses, and an independent reckoning for what happened on 20 July. These are not concessions to be won in some distant future. They are years overdue; they were owed to us before the first tear gas canister was fired, and we intend to collect them at the ballot box.
